posts.title: Myth-busting: "Azure backs everything up automatically."
posts.author: Flavio Quintela
posts.snippet:
Myth-busting: "Azure backs everything up automatically."

One of the most common misconceptions we hear when discussing Azure with customers is:

"We're in Azure, so we're backed up."

It's only partially true.

Azure does an incredible job protecting the underlying platform and provides a variety of resiliency, backup, and recovery capabilities. But under the shared responsibility model, protecting your data and ensuring it can be recovered when the unexpected happens is still your responsibility.

Azure can help protect against hardware failures, infrastructure issues, and data center outages. What it doesn't automatically protect you from is every scenario that actually causes organizations to lose data:
• Accidental deletion
• Ransomware encryption
• Misconfigured retention policies
• Application errors
• Bad deployments or human mistakes

Those risks still require a deliberate backup and recovery strategy. Many organizations mistakenly equate "cloud" with "backup." They're not the same thing. Just because data is hosted in Azure doesn't necessarily mean it can be recovered in the way your business would expect when something goes wrong. The technology may be available, but it still needs to be properly configured, monitored, tested, and aligned with business requirements.

posts.title: #KulisyAtaku: odpowiedzialność za dostawcę
posts.author: Grzegorz Kamiński
posts.snippet:
#KulisyAtaku: odpowiedzialność za dostawcę

Poniedziałek rano. Właścicielka przychodni otwiera laptopa.

System działa. Rejestracja przyjmuje pacjentów. Żadnego okna z żądaniem okupu, żadnego telefonu od informatyka. Wszystko wygląda normalnie.

Dane pacjentów — PESEL-e, recepty, historia leczenia — od kilku dni są już poza firmą.

Atak nie był na nią.

W ubiegły weekend cyberprzestępcy zaatakowali MyDr — dostawcę oprogramowania do zarządzania placówkami medycznymi. Wicepremier Krzysztof Gawkowski potwierdził skalę: około 19 milionów rekordów, ponad 2 TB danych. Więcej niż co drugi Polak.

Z systemu korzystało około 12 tysięcy placówek.

Powierzenie przetwarzania danych nie przenosi odpowiedzialności na dostawcę.

Przychodnia pozostaje administratorem. Odpowiada za wybór podmiotu przetwarzającego i za nadzór nad nim. Nawet jeśli to nie jej serwer padł.

Jak to wygląda w praktyce? 

W sprawie Fortum UODO nałożył na administratora karę prawie 5 mln zł. Na podmiot przetwarzający — 250 tys. zł. Dwudziestokrotna różnica. Przy wycieku danych 90 tysięcy osób.

Listopad 2023, ALAB Laboratoria: ransomware, dziesiątki tysięcy opublikowanych wyników badań, do 200 tysięcy zagrożonych pacjentów.

NIS2 i polska ustawa o KSC mówią o tym wprost: bezpieczeństwo łańcucha dostaw jest Twoim obowiązkiem. Nie obowiązkiem Twojego dostawcy.

Termin samorejestracji podmiotów: 3 października 2026.

Trzy pytania, na które warto znać odpowiedź, zanim zadzwoni do Ciebie dziennikarz albo UODO:

→ Który z Twoich dostawców przetwarza dane osobowe Twoich klientów? 
→ Kiedy ostatnio ktokolwiek zweryfikował, jak on te dane zabezpiecza — poza podpisaną umową powierzenia? 
→ Gdyby dziś wyciekły z jego systemu, ile czasu zajęłoby Ci ustalenie, czyje dokładnie?

Jeśli przy którymkolwiek z tych pytań się zawahałeś — napisz do mnie w wiadomości prywatnej.

posts.title: Day 74 of 90 with MyFirstHack. Threat actors — who attacks, and why.
posts.author: Tenzin Norden Thinley
posts.snippet:
Day 74 of 90 with MyFirstHack. Threat actors — who attacks, and why.

I've spent days learning HOW attacks work. Today: WHO is behind them — and it turns out the faceless "hacker" is actually several very different adversaries.

Cybercriminals want money, so they chase easy, profitable targets and move on if you're too hard. Nation-states (APTs) want specific secrets, so they target YOU specifically and persist for months — ordinary defences won't deter them. Hacktivists want to make a point. Insiders already have access. And the motivation explains everything: the target, the techniques, the goal, even whether they want to be noticed.

Today I learned how cybercriminals use automated ransomware while APTs custom-build zero-day exploits to quietly stay hidden for months.

The reassuring part: most of us face opportunistic criminals and automated attacks, not nation-states — and solid fundamentals (patching, good passwords, hardening) defeat the large majority of those. Defence is always defence against SOMEONE. Knowing who makes it focused.

16 days left.

Cyberattack Could Force KFC Store Closures

How prepared are you if threat actors hit your establishment? The possibility of KFC store closures caused by a recent cyberattack proves that even major brands aren't necessarily immune. 

The Disastrous Ripple Effects of a Cyberattack on Supplier Companies

On July 13, 2026, Nichirei Corporation, a large Japanese company that produces and distributes frozen and processed foods, reported widespread system failures due to unauthorized third-party access. The incident affected inbound and outbound cold-chain shipments for some corporate clients, including KFC.

The fast-food company's Japan outlets suffered shortages of chicken ingredients, prompting reduced menus, shortened hours, and temporary app suspensions before normal operations resumed. 

Assessing Third-Party Cybersecurity Risks

If one cyberattack on a supplier company can lead to possible KFC store closures, it's clear how interconnected cybersecurity truly is. Partnering with other companies for operations is a practical way to enhance efficiency, but it also introduces new vulnerabilities.

Third-party vendors usually have access to your critical systems or sensitive data, creating potential entry points for cyberattacks. A breach in one partner's network can quickly cascade into your own.

That's why it never hurts to review the cybersecurity posture of all your partners. Look for the following:

-Regularly practiced incident response plans
-Adherence to industry-standard security frameworks
-Routine vulnerability assessments and penetration testing
-Employee cybersecurity training and awareness programs

Strengthening Your Own Cybersecurity Measures for Business Continuity

If one of your partner companies experiences a cyberattack, having the following proactive measures in place can make all the difference.

Limit access: Give partners only the minimum system access they need to do their jobs, and employ multi-factor authentication when possible.

Isolate networks: With network segmentation, the infection cannot easily spread into your own core network if ever a partner's system gets hacked
.
Watch connections: Continuously track activity and data flow between your systems and vendors to spot strange behavior early.

Pre-stage "kill switches": Prepare emergency mechanisms to revoke API keys, shared tokens, or remote vendor access within minutes if a partner reports a breach.

Plan together: Include partner-failure scenarios in your emergency response plans so both sides know who to call and how to cut off access faster.

posts.title: I’ve seen a fairly predictable reaction to the Coldcard incident: self-custody is too dangerous, so serious holders should move their assets back to professional custodians.
posts.author: Artem Dikarev
posts.snippet:
I’ve seen a fairly predictable reaction to the Coldcard incident: self-custody is too dangerous, so serious holders should move their assets back to professional custodians.

I understand the instinct, but I’m not sure the conclusion follows.

The Coldcard problem goes back to firmware version 4.0.1, released in 2021. During a migration to a different cryptographic library, a configuration error meant that seed phrases could be generated using a predictable software source of randomness rather than proper hardware entropy.

To the user, everything looked normal. The device produced a valid BIP-39 seed phrase and the wallet behaved as expected. Underneath, however, the number of possible keys was far smaller than it should have been. That made offline reconstruction possible. No phishing, compromised exchange or physical access to the device was required.

The worst part is that a firmware update only fixes future key generation. It cannot add randomness to a seed created five years ago. Anyone affected has to move the assets to a genuinely new seed. Replacing the lock is of limited comfort when copies of the old key have been circulating for years.
I don’t see this as self-custody failing in principle. A critical component of its trust architecture failed. The user controlled the assets, but still had to trust the device to do what the documentation promised.

Moving to a custodian doesn’t remove the risk. It changes its form and introduces a counterparty.

The firmware risk is exchanged for internal-control failures, poor segregation of duties, commingling, sub-custodian exposure, operational outages and insolvency. There will also be a licence, auditors and a risk committee. On particularly fortunate occasions, there may even be minutes confirming that the subject was discussed.

That is why ESMA’s review of the operational resilience of crypto custodians is timely. It should look beyond the existence of a custody policy and examine how keys are generated, who can authorise transfers, how client assets are segregated and what happens when either the system or the provider fails.

Still, an ESMA checklist is not a sovereign guarantee. It may confirm that the controls have been documented and tested. It cannot promise that they’ll work at 3:17 a.m., when one provider is offline, another has been compromised, and the third is already speaking to its lawyers)

The sensible question isn’t whether custody involves trust. It’s which risks you’re accepting, whether you can monitor them, and what evidence supports the assurances you’ve been given.

A well-chosen custodian may give those risks a legal entity, financial statements, contractual accountability and meaningful insurance. Not every custodian deserves that confidence, and none should receive it without serious due diligence and ongoing monitoring.

An uncapped legal retainer helps too. It won’t reduce the risk, but it ensures somebody well-dressed can explain which exclusion it now belongs to.
posts.reason: Thoughtful technical analysis of custody risks by a recognized security figure invites engagement from compliance and legal audiences on a substantive policy question.

comments.text: The regulatory blind spot you're pointing at is real: custody audits tend to check whether a key-management policy exists, not whether the entropy source in the actual firmware build matches what the documentation claims - which is precisely the gap that let the Coldcard flaw persist since 2021 undetected.
Do you think ESMA's review will go as far as requiring reproducible builds or independent entropy testing for hardware wallets used by custodians, or will it stop at organisational controls?

In the disputes we get pulled into, the hardest cases to resolve are exactly this kind - not theft in the traditional sense, but a structural weakness in key generation that surfaces years later, by which point tracing the affected funds is far harder than tracing a straightforward hack.

🚨 COLDcard: $130M+ stolen, ~90% still sitting untouched 🚨 

Two weeks after the first wave, the scale of the Coldcard incident is becoming clearer.

1,719 BTC have been confirmed by Galaxy Research: approximately $111 million at the time of its analysis.

TRM Labs puts the figure at around 1,816 BTC, potentially making this the 3rd-largest crypto theft of 2026. The final total could exceed $130 million. 

But the most important number is not the amount stolen.

It is the amount that has not moved.

🔴 ~90% of the stolen BTC remains at the attackers' initial addresses.

The first three confirmed waves have not been meaningfully layered or mixed.

Only 64.9 BTC was deposited into Wasabi, while 200 ETH was sent to Tornado Cash on August 4.

On a theft exceeding 1,700 BTC, that is a tiny fraction.

Why?

Because stealing the assets is one problem.

Liquidating $100M+ of publicly tainted Bitcoin is another.

The attackers' addresses have already been shared with exchanges, blockchain analytics firms and US law enforcement. 

Any attempt to deposit the funds into a regulated exchange can therefore trigger automated risk controls.

And the blockchain is not just recording the theft.

It is recording the investigation.

TRM even identified OP_RETURN messages offering to launder the stolen funds for a 7% fee.

This case shows why blockchain intelligence is not simply about following transactions.

It is about understanding when funds move, how they move, where they move, and what infrastructure they interact with.

At Indago Labs, this is precisely the type of intelligence we build for financial institutions, investigators and legal teams.

The bigger the stolen amount, the harder it becomes to spend without leaving a trail.

🚨 **THE MONEY MULE NETWORK: One Account. Many Victims. Bigger Crime.**

A money mule may appear to be an ordinary customer—but their account can become a critical link in a much larger criminal network.

Criminals recruit people through **fake jobs, social media, online ads, romance scams and personal connections**, then use their accounts to receive, move or withdraw illicit funds.

### 🔎 HOW MONEY MULE NETWORKS WORK

**Recruitment → Account Opening → Illicit Funds Deposited → Rapid Movement → Layering → Cash/crypto Conversion → Criminal Network**

### 🚩 RED FLAGS AML PROFESSIONALS SHOULD WATCH

🔹 Newly opened accounts with immediate high-value activity
🔹 Rapid incoming and outgoing transfers
🔹 Multiple unrelated sources sending funds
🔹 Frequent cash withdrawals after receiving credits
🔹 Transfers involving unusual or high-risk locations
🔹 Use of VPNs, proxies or unfamiliar devices
🔹 Account activity inconsistent with the customer's profile
🔹 Students, unemployed individuals or customers with no clear source of income suddenly receiving large volumes of funds

### 🛡️ HOW FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS CAN RESPOND

✔️ Monitor account-opening patterns
✔️ Analyse transaction behaviour and velocity
✔️ Use advanced transaction-monitoring capabilities
✔️ Combine internal data with external intelligence
✔️ Investigate and escalate suspicious activity
✔️ Share intelligence where appropriate
✔️ Act quickly to disrupt confirmed mule activity
✔️ Continuously update controls as typologies evolve

📌 **KEY TAKEAWAY:**
Behind every mule account, there may be a victim, a scam and a larger criminal network.

**One account can become a gateway to fraud, money laundering and other serious financial crimes.**

posts.author: Sean Parkin
posts.snippet:
Nine and a half years. 212 successful projects. More P1s than I could count if I tried.

Today is my last day at Millgate.

The numbers are the easy part to write down. What they don't capture is the people I did it with - and in my case that has usually meant the client's own IT teams.

The operations manager still in the building at two in the morning. The finance director deciding, there and then, what the business could stand to be without until Monday. 

You learn a great deal about an organisation on nights like that, and a fair amount about yourself.

Most of my work has been solo. One person on the client's side of the table, being the one they ring first. It's a privilege and it's a discipline in equal measure: there's no committee to hide behind when you have to tell someone their backups aren't what they think they are, or that the thing they've been quoted for isn't the thing they actually need.

The moment I'll keep forever is a stage. An auditorium full of clients, and a slot to show how a ransomware attack really unfolds - "From Breach to Blackout" - with live demonstrations of the tools and techniques attackers use. 

Not slides about risk. The thing itself, in front of them. You could hear the room change. Nothing else I've ever done has moved so many businesses from "we should probably look at that" to "we're absolutely doing this right now" so quickly.

To Millgate: thank you for nine and a half years, for the trust, and for the room to do the work properly.  Your support while I move on to fulfil my ambitions is all that I could ask for.

To the clients who let me into the best and the worst nights of their year, and then asked me back: thank you.

Nine and a half years leaves you with firm views about how this work ought to be done.

I'm going off to act on mine.

More on Monday.

posts.title: Bismillah,
posts.author: Ika Kartika Sari
posts.snippet:
Bismillah,

continued

External vs. Internal Audit: 

Methodology and Operations when examining how audits are conducted, understanding the distinct roles of internal and external auditors is essential.

While both aim to ensure corporate accountability, their methodologies, fieldwork techniques, and reporting styles differ significantly.

​Here is of how they compare across three core areas:

​1. Planning and Scoping

​Internal Audit (Risk-Based Approach):
Internal auditors utilize Risk-Based Internal Auditing (RBIA). 
They map out business processes most vulnerable to fraud, inefficiency, or operational failure. 
Their scope is highly flexible—shifting seamlessly from supply chain efficiency one week to IT compliance or branch operations the next.

​External Audit (Financial Statement Risk Approach):
External auditors focus strictly on the Risk of Material Misstatement. 
Their planning centers on high-risk financial areas prone to human error or fraud. 
Their scope is structured and rigid, always revolving around core accounting cycles (sales/receivables, purchases/payables, inventory, cash, and fixed assets).

​2. Fieldwork and Testing Techniques

​Internal Audit (Operational & Compliance Testing):
The fieldwork involves deep dives into operational realities and procedural compliance. 
Techniques include direct observation, unannounced physical inspections, in-depth staff interviews, workflow walkthroughs, and evaluating internal control effectiveness.

​External Audit (Substantive & Analytical Procedures):
Fieldwork centers heavily on financial figures and supporting documents. Methods include vouching and tracing, direct confirmations with third parties (such as banks, customers, and vendors), and mathematical testing of financial calculations.

​3. Reporting and Follow-Up

​Internal Audit (Constructive & Continuous):
Reports are internal, detailed, and aimed at operational improvement. 
They highlight root causes and practical recommendations. 
Crucially, the job doesn't end at publication; 
internal auditors actively perform follow-up audits to ensure management implements the suggested fixes.

​External Audit (Formal & Public-Facing):
Reports are standardized, formal, and intended for external stakeholders. 
Formats are strictly regulated, culminating in an Audit Opinion (such as Unqualified/Clean) alongside a separate Management Letter. 
Once delivered to shareholders or regulators, the external auditor's duty is complete—they do not monitor daily operational fixes.
​
​In short, internal audits act as an ongoing compass for operational health and risk management from within, whereas external audits serve as an independent financial health check for the outside world.

- IKS -

posts.title: On 4 August 2024, I opened Regulation (EU) 2024/1787 for a gas procurement team expecting another reporting burden.
posts.author: Prajjwal Kaushik
posts.snippet:
On 4 August 2024, I opened Regulation (EU) 2024/1787 for a gas procurement team expecting another reporting burden.

The real answer sat inside its supply contracts, not its sustainability report.

I had assumed methane rules would stay with operators inside Europe. Measure leaks. Repair equipment. Send records.

Then I reached the import provisions.

A shipment could clear commercially and still carry weak methane evidence.

That line changed how I saw the rule.

The mechanism moves in stages. EU importers collect producer and exporter information.

From 2027, new and renewed contracts must carry equivalent measurement and verification evidence.

By 2030, methane intensity limits reach imported oil, gas, and coal. The border starts moving upstream.

This is not only a climate disclosure task.

We check price.
We check volume.
We check delivery.
Now we must check how the producer measured methane.

Here is what I learned while tracing that chain.

A buyer needs the producing asset, not only the trading company.
A buyer needs the measurement method, not only a final number.
A buyer needs contract rights when evidence fails, not only a supplier promise.

The UNEP Oil and Gas Methane Partnership 2.0 already points toward source-level reporting and reconciliation.

Regulation 2024/1787 gives that evidence commercial weight.

Yes, the EU can call this market protection and emissions control.

But that misses the wider shift.

Brussels wrote the rule, but it can change monitoring at a field far beyond Europe. It works because the buyer controls market access.

The quiet truth nobody says out loud?

The sustainability team cannot fix a weak purchase contract after the cargo moves.

We ended with a different checklist. Legal owned evidence clauses. Procurement owned supplier questions. Operations checked measurement boundaries.

The report came last.

I began with a disclosure rule on my screen. I left seeing a new condition for entering the market.

Are we still treating methane data as reporting when it has already become part of the product?

posts.title: I'm all for helping a company improve it's products (as many of you know) and as such had signed up as a beta tester for an home automation product. So far so good.
posts.author: Richard Fry
posts.snippet:
I'm all for helping a company improve it's products (as many of you know) and as such had signed up as a beta tester for an home automation product. So far so good.

Yesterday I received an email thanking me for my interest and asking if I was still interested in testing their product - if so there was a fully refundable $99 fee, which would be returned to me after I had completed the trial and provided the required level of feedback.

Now, this in itself isn't that odd as I can understand the desire to protect their investment and ensure participants don't just take the product and not provide the feedback required.

Now the red flags
1. Asking for money up front 
2. The sending email address is an iCloud redirect "hide my email" address with a name field of the COO of the company in question.
3. The value they are asking for is just below the section 75 credit card protection limit.

Now, this could all be legitimate and the email address could be an individualised one to allow tracking of responses.

Or

Their register of prospects who expressed an interest in beta testing their product has been compromised and this is an elaborate phishing scam.

(Also not helped that to contact the COO of the company on here I need to either tag them publicly or subscribe to LI premium to allow me to message them).

Thoughts ........
posts.reason: Individual sharing suspected phishing/fraud detection experience and explicitly seeking input, which could invite discussion but targets a distressed person rather than institutional buyers.

comments.text: The email address mismatch is the strongest signal here — a legitimate COO's outreach for a beta program almost never routes through a personal iCloud relay address, that's a classic sign of a compromised contact list being used for outreach.
Did the payment request specify a payment method, and if so was it card, bank transfer or crypto — that alone often tells you a lot about how traceable or reversible any loss would be?

The 'just under the chargeback protection limit' detail is a pattern we see constantly in scam structuring, whether it's card protection thresholds or reporting thresholds for financial institutions — it is almost never coincidental.

posts.title: Tariffs went up. Factory jobs didn't come back. Now it's someone else's fault.
posts.author: MeridianFront
posts.snippet:
Tariffs went up. Factory jobs didn't come back. Now it's someone else's fault.

The White House just put out a report saying the reason tariffs haven't brought back US factory jobs is because of a big "scam." The claim: Chinese companies are secretly sending their goods through other countries first, so they can dodge US tariffs on China. The report calls it "industrial-scale customs fraud."That's a strong claim. So let's look at what the actual numbers say.

→ Factory jobs: Still haven't gone back to where they were before 2018, when the first round of China tariffs hit. And it's worse in Rust Belt states like Ohio, Michigan, and Pennsylvania — job losses there are deeper than the rest of the country.
→ New factories: Spending on building new manufacturing plants peaked in 2024 and has been falling since. If tariffs were working, you'd expect this number to keep climbing, not drop.
→ Foreign investment: In 2025, foreign companies spent only $4.6B building brand new US plants, and $9.6B expanding existing ones. That's a small number for an economy the size of the US. Foreign companies don't seem convinced yet.
→ Hiring problems: 44% of US manufacturers say they're struggling to find and keep good workers. That's a real, homegrown problem tariffs can't fix.
→ About the "fraud": Transshipment (routing goods through a third country to dodge tariffs) isn't new, and the US already has a program running to catch it. Even the White House's own report admits its evidence is more "suggestive" than "proven." Nobody is saying zero fraud happens — the question is whether it happens at a scale big enough to explain why the whole tariff policy hasn't delivered.

Here's the simple logic that gets missed: when a tariff makes Chinese goods more expensive, a US buyer doesn't have to switch to a US supplier. They have other options too — buy from Vietnam, India, Mexico, Korea, or Europe instead. No cheating required, no rules broken. Just a buyer picking the next cheapest option that isn't China.

If US factories aren't winning that shifted demand, the more useful question is: why not? Price? Speed? Quality? Capacity? Workforce shortages? That's a harder conversation than "foreign companies are cheating us" — but it's the one that actually explains what's happening.

For anyone working in supply chain or trade policy, this is a good reminder: rerouted trade and reshored trade are not the same thing. Worth checking which one you're actually looking at before taking a headline at face value.

2.  **Leadership Alignment:** Leaders who model the behavior they expect from their teams.
3.  **Environmental Design:** Creating a workspace that supports human performance rather than draining it.

Stop buying "wellness" and start building a high-performance culture. One is a cost; the other is an investment in enterprise value.

A victim was scammed. Cryptocurrency was sent. Did the officer get the right information to get the case moving?

That's the problem Crypto for Patrol was designed to address.

When I was going full speed with my training company, Fintech Focus Training & Consulting and working as a Financial Crimes Detective at the same time, I began development of this this course based largely on what I was seeing firsthand as a Financial Crimes Detective.

I worked numerous cryptocurrency-related fraud investigations, traced transactions, worked with exchanges and prosecutors, and in one case helped recover approximately $29,000 in cryptocurrency for an elderly couple who had been scammed.

One thing became very clear:

The initial contact with the victim matters. And so does time.

Cryptocurrency can move quickly. Delays can reduce opportunities to trace funds and potentially recover assets for victims.

That's where patrol comes in.

Crypto for Patrol isn't designed to turn patrol officers into blockchain analysts.

It's practical, action-oriented training focused on fraud and scam cases involving cryptocurrency.

The goal is for officers to leave knowing how to:

• Recognize the cryptocurrency element of a fraud or scam
• Conduct an effective initial response
• Gather the critical information needed to get the case moving
• Properly document that information in the initial report
• Understand enough about cryptocurrency and blockchain to know why those actions matter

This isn't “What is Bitcoin?” training.

It's about knowing what to DO when the victim is sitting in front of you or calling on the phone to make a report.

One thing I consistently heard from officers who attended my cryptocurrency training was:

“You made this easy to understand.”

That was always the goal.

I want to offer this training because I keep seeing the same problem: victims are still losing money through cryptocurrency-related scams, and the information gathered during that first law enforcement contact can have a real impact on what happens next.

I'd like to offer Crypto for Patrol as a live online law enforcement training.
Before I put a date on the calendar, though, I want to gauge the interest.

If you're an officer who would attend, comment “INTERESTED” or message me.

If you're a Sergeant, Lieutenant, Captain, Commander, training coordinator or someone who influences training at your agency, I'd especially like to hear from you. Message me and let me know approximately how many officers from your agency you think would attend.

I'm not asking for a commitment. I'm simply gauging interest before putting a date on the calendar.

posts.title: 🚨 MAJOR CRYPTO SECURITY ALERT: Trezor customer names, phone numbers, emails AND home addresses have been exposed in a third-party data breach.
posts.author: efani
posts.snippet:
🚨 MAJOR CRYPTO SECURITY ALERT: Trezor customer names, phone numbers, emails AND home addresses have been exposed in a third-party data breach.

Trezor says shipping provider ShipMonk experienced a breach affecting 13,689 customers.

For 11,742 customers, the exposed information included their full name, email address, phone number and shipping address. Another 1,947 customers had partial information exposed.

Trezor’s own systems and hardware wallets were not compromised.

But this is still an unusually sensitive dataset for crypto holders.

A normal ecommerce breach might tell an attacker where someone shops. This breach can potentially tell them that a specific person recently purchased a hardware wallet, while also giving them the phone number, email address and physical location associated with that purchase.

That makes targeted attacks much easier to personalize.

A convincing phishing email can reference the victim’s real purchase. A fake support agent may already know their name and phone number. The information could also be useful for impersonation or SIM-swap attempts.

And there is a physical-security dimension that should not be dismissed.

Hardware wallets are commonly associated with self-custody of cryptocurrency. When ownership can be connected to a home address, the threat model can extend beyond malware and phishing into robbery, extortion and wrench-attack risk.

No physical attacks have been linked to this breach at this point. But exposing home addresses belonging to identifiable hardware-wallet customers creates a risk that did not exist before the data leaked.

This also comes during a difficult period for hardware-wallet security. The recent Coldcard incident involved a completely different technical problem, and Trezor’s devices were not compromised here.

The broader lesson is still important:

Protecting the hardware wallet itself is only one part of protecting the person who owns it.

Manufacturers need to treat fulfillment providers, customer databases, shipping records and data-retention policies as part of the security perimeter.

Trezor’s 90-day data-retention policy helped limit how far back this breach could reach.

If you received Trezor’s notification, be especially suspicious of unexpected calls, texts and emails claiming to be from Trezor.

Never enter your recovery seed on a website. Never provide it to “support.” Verify communications independently through Trezor’s official channels.

posts.title: Ransomware just got a decentralized upgrade—takedowns are now nearly impossible.
posts.author: Omar Ahmed
posts.snippet:
Ransomware just got a decentralized upgrade—takedowns are now nearly impossible.

DeadLock is rewriting the extortion playbook using Polygon smart contracts. Traditional ransomware infrastructure relies on centralized servers that law enforcement can seize. DeadLock’s approach? It stores proxy server URLs and data leak blog content directly on the blockchain.

  The Problem:  
- Attackers need resilient communication channels to negotiate and leak data
- Centralized domains and servers are easy targets for takedown operations
- Victims need a way to contact operators, but that channel must survive disruption

  The Agitation:  
Microsoft Threat Intelligence confirms DeadLock embeds a full interactive HTML recovery chat inside every encrypted system. This single-page app handles end-to-end encrypted messaging, a paginated data leak blog, and a file browser—no backend server required.

Here’s the technical twist:
- JavaScript inside the HTML note calls Polygon smart contracts to fetch fresh proxy server addresses
- Operators rotate these URLs without touching victim-facing domains or registering new ones
- Leaked files are hosted on the blockchain via the Wasabi protocol, browsable without a web server

This isn’t just obfuscation. It’s censorship-resistant infrastructure. Group-IB notes attackers can apply “infinite variants” of this technique because smart contracts are immutable and globally distributed.

  The Solution:  
DeadLock’s hybrid crypto design combines Curve25519 elliptic-curve cryptography with the XChaCha20 stream cipher for file encryption. It also uses geofencing to avoid execution in CIS and select Middle Eastern countries, plus resource-aware throttling to stay under the radar during encryption.

Since July 2025, DeadLock has claimed 96 victims across Italy, Spain, Poland, Türkiye, and the U.S. The group isn’t tied to known affiliate programs, keeping its profile low while its infrastructure stays resilient.

How is your team securing your infrastructure against this type of exploitation? Let’s discuss in the comments below.

#Ransomware #BlockchainSecurity #ThreatIntelligence

posts.title: NIST's post-quantum signature bake-off just lost a finalist — and today is the deadline for the other eight to prove they won't be next.
posts.author: Gerald Beuchelt
posts.snippet:
NIST's post-quantum signature bake-off just lost a finalist — and today is the deadline for the other eight to prove they won't be next.

On July 29, HAWK's own team withdrew it from NIST's Additional Digital Signatures process after confirming an attack from Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview model that cut HAWK-256's estimated key-recovery cost from 2^64 to a demonstrated 2^38, roughly halving its security margin. The AI-driven attack took about 60 hours and about $100,000 in compute. HAWK had cleared two rounds of expert human review since 2022. Today, August 14, is NIST's deadline for the remaining eight round-three candidates — FAEST, MAYO, MQOM, QR-UOV, SDitH, SNOVA, SQIsign, and UOV — to file finalized specifications ahead of a two-year evaluation window and the 2027 standardization conference.

The process worked as designed. Standardization exists to surface weak candidates before deployment, and HAWK's elimination, like SIKE's collapse in the last contest, is the system catching a flaw early, not a crisis. **The story is the timeline compression, not the algorithm.** Two years of coordinated human peer review missed a lattice symmetry that one AI model, working largely on its own, found in 60 hours. Anthropic says verification, not discovery, was the actual bottleneck: confirming the result took its own researchers weeks.

**If you own crypto-agility or PQC migration planning, this is your prompt to ask vendors a new question:** has their algorithm choice been tested against AI-assisted cryptanalysis, not just historical human review? Build re-evaluation checkpoints into migration roadmaps that assumed a stable candidate pool.

Full research: https://lnkd.in/dUF4vUrw

If an AI model can do in 60 hours what two years of NIST-coordinated review didn't, how often should your organization be re-testing the cryptography it already trusts?

posts.title: Here's what I want to be true in five years.
posts.author: Jake Hall
posts.snippet:
Here's what I want to be true in five years.

A local shop owner needs £30k to bring in a container of stock.

He doesn't go to a bank.

Eleven people from his community fund it between them. If the stock sells, they share the profit. If it doesn't, they share the loss.

The contracts, the company structure, the tax treatment and the accounts are generated in an afternoon.

None of that is technically hard. It's just expensive.

Structuring a genuine profit sharing deal properly costs thousands in legal and tax fees. Nobody can justify that on a £30k deal. So it either doesn't happen, or it happens on a handshake and falls apart the moment something goes wrong.

Banks won't fix this. Interest is the product. Capital rules punish real risk sharing.

I'm not trying to build a bank.

I'm trying to build blueprints.

Legally sound, tax efficient, zero interest structures that a small business and a handful of people who believe in it can run between themselves. Open source, free to use.

This has been rattling around my head for years. I'm finally giving it my weekends.

Right now I just want to find out whether anyone else wants it. Two things I'm looking for:

→ An SME that needs £20k to £100k and would rather share profit than pay interest. Stock, equipment, a specific project. Anything with a clear use of funds.

→ Anyone who would put £2k to £10k into a local business they can actually see and understand, on profit share terms instead of a fixed return.

There's nothing to sign and nothing to buy. I want 20 honest conversations about how people really fund things and where it breaks down.

If that's you, or you know someone it might be, comment below or drop me a DM.

P.S. If you're a lawyer, accountant or tax adviser and this sounds like a fun problem, I'd love 30 minutes of your brain.
posts.reason: Open-source legal framework for profit-sharing capital structures addresses genuine institutional friction point; relevant to lawyers and compliance teams exploring alternative funding mechanisms.

comments.text: The part that will actually determine whether this scales isn't the legal template, it's the source-of-funds question for the eleven contributors — any profit-share vehicle that touches multiple unrelated funders will eventually need some standard way to document where their capital came from, or it becomes unbankable in exactly the way informal handshake deals already are.

Have you thought through how disputes over loss allocation get resolved when it's eleven individual contributors rather than a single lender — who arbitrates if the shop owner and the group disagree on why the stock didn't sell?

We deal with the aftermath of exactly this kind of informal profit-share arrangement gone wrong in asset tracing work — the absence of clear documentation at the outset is almost always what turns a simple loss into a years-long dispute.

posts.title: Reviva $RVPH pushed its Phase 3 back in Q2. The trial that was supposed to start enrolling this quarter now starts in H1 2027, and the FDA feedback ahead of it moved from mid-2026
posts.author: Fajasy @StableBread
posts.snippet:
Reviva $RVPH pushed its Phase 3 back in Q2. The trial that was supposed to start enrolling this quarter now starts in H1 2027, and the FDA feedback ahead of it moved from mid-2026 to Q4 2026.

Here's where four catalysts stand since my Reviva write-up in June:
1) FDA feedback on the new form of brilaroxazine. I had it in late July or August off an 8-12 week comment in late May. It's now Q4 2026.
2) RECOVER-2 enrollment was Q3 2026. It's now H1 2027, and explicitly "subject to receipt of additional financing."
3) Still "pursuing partnership opportunities" for the pipeline. The 10-Q's version of that is a collaboration where Reviva relinquishes rights to its technologies or future revenue in exchange for funding. Nothing signed, and no committed external sources of capital.
4) The Phase 3 readout I had in Q4 2027 now completes "in 2028," which on my read pushes the NDA into 2029 and approval to around 2030.

The trial data itself didn't change. But all of it was generated on the old drug substance, and Reviva plans to run RECOVER-2 on a new one. What moved is when any of it can turn into an approval, and that's now roughly a year later than expected.

That's why the patent work matters more now, not less.

The original brilaroxazine patents expire in 2030. Reviva says the first US one "may be extendable up to 2035" if the drug is approved. So on a 2030 approval, and only if that extension comes through, an acquirer is buying ~5 years of exclusivity. That doesn't fund a label expansion into bipolar and depression.

The fix is the new form, a different drug substance and a different formulation, which is what Reviva is trying to patent separately.

It moved forward on August 11. The provisional was already in as of Q1, and what's new is that Reviva filed the full composition of matter application internationally through PCT and put the US version on the USPTO's Track One fast track.

Two caveats to know:
1) Track One targets a final disposition within ~12 months of prioritized status being granted, and a final disposition can be a rejection rather than a grant.
2) The 10-Q flags that the FDA may require additional Phase 3 work specifically because Reviva is switching to the new form.

So Q4 2026 is the next date that matters. FDA feedback comes first, the bioequivalence study follows, and enrollment only starts in H1 2027 if Reviva has the money by then.

The patent runs on its own clock. Reviva can start the trial without a granted patent, and it can get the patent granted without starting the trial.

You can read $RVPH's recent 10-Q for free here: https://lnkd.in/ef-9-zH2

posts.title: A crypto licence does not automatically make a business bankable
posts.author: Harrison Alderidge
posts.snippet:
A crypto licence does not automatically make a business bankable
One of the recent developments in the UK crypto market caught my attention.
British lawmakers have raised concerns that difficulties crypto companies face in accessing banking services could ultimately restrict the growth of the sector.
And I think this highlights an important issue that goes beyond the UK.
We often discuss crypto regulation in terms of licences, registrations and regulatory frameworks. But obtaining the appropriate authorisation is only one part of building a functioning crypto business.
A bank conducts its own risk assessment.
It will look at the ownership structure, jurisdictions involved, source of funds, transaction flows, target markets, counterparties, AML controls and the overall business model. A regulated company can therefore still find itself struggling with banking.
For founders, I think there is a practical lesson here: banking should not be something you start thinking about after the regulatory structure has already been built.
The licence, corporate structure, banking and payment infrastructure should ideally be considered together from the beginning.
Otherwise, it is entirely possible to create a compliant regulatory structure that is difficult to operate in practice.
The UK situation is a good reminder of the growing gap between being regulated and being bankable — and why both matter when building a crypto business.

In the cases you've seen, is it usually the ownership structure or the transaction flow history that trips up the banking application, once the licence itself is no longer the sticking point?

posts.title: Daubert doesn't ask if a method sounds trustworthy. It asks four specific things: can it be tested, what's the error rate, has it been peer reviewed, is it generally accepted.
posts.author: Craig Solomon
posts.snippet:
Daubert doesn't ask if a method sounds trustworthy. It asks four specific things: can it be tested, what's the error rate, has it been peer reviewed, is it generally accepted.

SHA-256 clears all four without much of an argument. It's been tested under public scrutiny for well over a decade. The error rate for a collision, two different files producing the same hash, is effectively zero, computed and published, not asserted by a vendor. NIST standardized it. Every forensic toolkit on the market uses it for exactly this purpose: proving a file hasn't changed since it was captured.

That's a stronger starting position than most digital evidence methods walk into court with. Compare it to a metadata field an operating system wrote, one a user could edit with the right software. Or a timestamp embedded in a file that doesn't survive a re-export.

I think the mistake is treating "blockchain" as the thing under Daubert scrutiny. It isn't. The hash function is the thing under scrutiny, and hash functions carry thirty years of published, peer-reviewed literature behind them. The chain just gives that hash a place to live that no single party controls.

If you're an expert witness defending a digital evidence method under Daubert, which piece of the methodology actually worries you: the hash, the chain, or the custody gap in between?

comments.text: C'est exactement ça la distinction qui compte: le hachage prouve l'intégrité, la chaîne prouve la non-répudiation du timing, et c'est la lacune de chain of custody entre la saisie initiale des données on-chain et le rapport final qui reste souvent le point faible attaqué en contre-interrogatoire.

posts.author: Ranjith Kumar Tirumalasetti
posts.snippet:
🚀 Introducing EvidenceChain — Protecting Truth. Preserving Justice.

We’re excited to share EvidenceChain, a blockchain-powered digital evidence protection and verification platform that we built as part of the MIC Hackfest.

Digital evidence such as CCTV footage, images, videos, forensic reports, and documents plays a critical role in investigations and legal proceedings. But one important question remains:

How can we prove that digital evidence has not been tampered with?

💡 Our Solution — EvidenceChain

EvidenceChain creates a cryptographic proof for every piece of digital evidence and enables its authenticity to be verified through a transparent and tamper-evident workflow.

🔐 Key Technologies:

• SHA-256 — Generates a unique cryptographic fingerprint for each evidence file
• IPFS — Enables decentralized storage of evidence
• Blockchain — Maintains an immutable evidence record and verification trail
• x402 — Enables secure, automated pay-per-use access to verification services
• Automated Verification — Compares the current evidence hash with the original blockchain record

🔄 How it works:

Evidence Upload
→ SHA-256 Hash Generation
→ Evidence Storage
→ Blockchain Registration
→ Evidence ID
→ Verification Request
→ Hash Comparison
→ Authentic / Tampered

What makes this project meaningful to us is the combination of Blockchain + Cryptography + Decentralized Storage + x402 into a single workflow focused on a real-world problem.

🎯 Potential Applications

👮 Police & Criminal Investigations
⚖️ Courts & Legal Proceedings
🧪 Forensic Laboratories
🛡️ Cyber Crime Investigations
🏢 Insurance Fraud Investigation
🏛️ Government & Institutional Evidence Management

This project was built collaboratively by Ranjith & Hafi — Team GenesisX for MIC Hackfest.

A huge learning experience for us in understanding how emerging technologies like Blockchain and x402 can be applied beyond finance to solve problems involving trust, integrity, and verification.

When evidence matters, trust should be verifiable.
